definition: Theocratic means governed by religious authority or leaders.
task: Write one sentence of your own using the word theocratic. Make the sentence show what the word means -- a reader who did not know theocratic should be able to work it out from your sentence.
avoid_verbatim: The strategy game's theocratic faction is the fan favorite: temples collect the taxes, and a council of oracles can veto the king's wars.
A religious society is full of faith — far short of theocratic, since believers can keep their courts and their altars in different buildings.
Clerical influence puts clergy in the corridors of power, advising and administering, but it stops short of theocratic until the clergy stop advising the rulers and become them.

Priestly describes what belongs to or befits priests — priestly robes, priestly duties, a priestly calm. It says nothing about power. Theocratic is a claim about the state itself: the clergy do not just serve at the altar, they govern — writing laws, judging cases, collecting taxes.

Church-run is the plain, literal label for the arrangement theocratic names: religious officials hold the levers. Use church-run for a school or a hospital; when a whole government answers to the temple, theocratic is the formal word historians and political scientists reach for.

Theocratic means governed by religious authority or leaders.
Medieval Durham came close to theocratic rule in practice — its prince-bishop minted coins, raised an army, and judged criminals, holding the crozier in one hand and the county in the other.

Theocratic is more precise than 'religious' because a nation full of believers is religious; it becomes theocratic only when religious authority holds the levers of state — writing the laws, staffing the courts, crowning or canceling the king.
Theocratic classifies governments, real and fictional — reach for it when religious authority actually rules, not merely inspires.
A devout country with secular courts isn't theocratic.
